hints: Look at what functional group is lost and gained in each step, for example $\text{OH}$ to $\text{Br}$ means $\text{OH}$ must be converted into a better leaving group.
Recall how tertiary alcohols are converted to bromoalkanes using bromide ion in strong acid, and how bromoalkanes are converted back using aqueous alkali.
Think about what reagent removes water from an alcohol to form an alkene, hot concentrated acid or hot aluminium oxide.
Consider what happens when $\text{HBr}$ adds across a $\text{C=C}$ double bond and whether any other reagent is needed.

Match each change to the list: swapping $\text{OH}$ for $\text{Br}$ is substitution, adding water across $\text{C-Br}$ is hydrolysis, losing water is dehydration, adding across $\text{C=C}$ is addition.
walkthrough:
Sort out reaction 1, alcohol to bromoalkane**
You are going from $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{COH}$ to $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$. The $\text{OH}$ group is swapped for $\text{Br}$, so this is substitution. $\text{OH}^{-}$ is a poor leaving group, so you need acid plus a source of $\text{Br}^{-}$. In AS chemistry that is concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ or $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ with $\text{NaBr}$, or simply $\text{HBr}$, or red $\text{P}$ with $\text{Br}_{2}$.

Sort out reaction 2, bromoalkane back to alcohol**
This is the reverse, $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$ to $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{COH}$. Again $\text{Br}$ is swapped for $\text{OH}$, so substitution, but now water is effectively adding $\text{OH}$ across the $\text{C-Br}$ bond, so it is also called hydrolysis. The classic reagent is aqueous or dilute $\text{NaOH}$ or $\text{KOH}$, usually warmed. Do not write ethanolic, that would give elimination.

Sort out reaction 3, alcohol to alkene**
Here $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{COH}$ loses $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to give $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$. Losing water is dehydration. You need a dehydrating agent with heat: concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ or $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$, or pass vapour over hot $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$, pumice or porous pot.

Sort out reaction 4, alkene to bromoalkane**
Now $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ gains $\text{H}$ and $\text{Br}$ to give two bromo isomers. Adding across $\text{C=C}$ is addition. The only reagent needed is $\text{HBr}$, no catalyst. Two products form because $\text{H}^{+}$ can add to either end of the double bond.

Final answer: Reaction 1: conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ / $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ with $\text{NaBr}$ OR $\text{P}$ / $\text{Br}_{2}$ OR $\text{HBr}$; substitution.
Reaction 2: aqueous / dilute $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{KOH}$; substitution and hydrolysis.
Reaction 3: conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ / $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ OR $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ / $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ / pumice, heat; dehydration.
Reaction 4: $\text{HBr}$; addition.

hints: Start by showing why the $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks on its own, think about bond polarity and where the bonding electrons go.
Recall the two steps of $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$: slow ionisation to a carbocation then fast attack by the nucleophile.
Remember to show the lone pair on $\text{OH}^{-}$, the positive charge on the central carbon, and curly arrows starting from electrons, not atoms.
walkthrough:
Show the slow ionisation**
Draw $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C-Br}$ with the dipole $^{\delta+}\text{C}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ because $\text{Br}$ is more electronegative than $\text{C}$. Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and pointing to $\text{Br}$. That shows heterolytic fission. You form the tertiary carbocation $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+}$ with a full positive charge on carbon, plus $\text{Br}^{-}$.

Show fast nucleophilic attack**
Now bring in $:\text{OH}^{-}$ with its lone pairs shown. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on oxygen straight to the $\text{C}^{+}$ centre. The oxygen donates its pair to form the new $\text{C-O}$ bond, giving $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{COH}$.

Check the SN1 essentials**
There are only two arrows in total, no simultaneous attack. Charges balance: $+1$ and $-1$ on each side of step 2. Lone pairs, dipoles, charges and arrows are all included, which is what earns the three marks.

Final answer: Step 1: $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+} + \text{Br}^{-}$, curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$.
Step 2: $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+} + :\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{COH}$, curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{OH}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{+}$.

hints: Start from the word isomer, what must stay the same for two molecules to be isomers?
Think about what must be different if they are structural rather than stereo isomers, the connectivity, not the 3D arrangement.
Recall one type where the carbon skeleton branches differently, for example butane and methylpropane.
Recall the other two types, one where the same functional group moves position and one where the functional group itself changes.
walkthrough:
Pin down the same part**
Isomers always share the same molecular formula. For $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Br}$, both 1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane contain 4 carbons, 9 hydrogens and 1 bromine. Same numbers of each atom.

Pin down the different part**
Structural means the atoms are joined in a different order. So the structural or displayed formula is different. This is different from stereoisomerism where connectivity is the same but arrangement in space differs.

Name the three families**
Chain or skeletal: carbon backbone differs, straight versus branched. Positional: same skeleton and same functional group but group is on a different carbon, for example 1-bromobutane versus 2-bromobutane. Functional group: different functional group, for example an alcohol versus an ether.

Final answer: Structural isomers are different molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural / displayed formulae.
Three types: chain / skeletal isomerism, positional / regioisomerism, functional group isomerism.

hints: Compare the structures, 1-bromobutane is primary while $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$ is tertiary, which mechanism favours primary substrates?
Think about what intermediate would have to form in $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ and whether a primary carbocation is stable enough.
Link stability to alkyl groups, more alkyl groups give more electron donation by the positive inductive effect.
walkthrough:
Identify the new mechanism**
Reaction 2 with $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$ is $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ because the tertiary carbocation is stable. 1-bromobutane $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$ is primary, so it reacts by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$, a one step nucleophilic substitution where $\text{OH}^{-}$ attacks as $\text{Br}^{-}$ leaves.

Explain why SN1 fails**
$\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ needs a relatively stable carbocation intermediate. A primary carbocation $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$ has no stabilisation and is too high in energy to form at a reasonable rate.

Link to inductive effect**
Alkyl groups push electrons toward the positive centre, the $+\text{I}$ effect. The tertiary cation has three methyl groups donating electron density, spreading the positive charge. The primary system has only one alkyl group, so much less donation, much less stability, hence the switch to $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$.

Final answer: Mechanism: $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ / nucleophilic substitution (bimolecular).
No stable carbocation / intermediate is formed.
1-bromobutane has only one alkyl group so less $+\text{I}$ inductive electron donation than the tertiary substrate, primary carbocation too unstable, so concerted mechanism occurs.

hints: Recall the two kinds of stereoisomerism at AS level, optical needing a chiral centre and cis-trans needing different groups on each end of $\text{C=C}$.
Look closely at $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$, what groups are attached to the left carbon and to the right carbon?
walkthrough:
Rule out optical isomerism**
For optical isomerism you need a chiral carbon with four different groups. Methylpropene $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ has only three carbons in the double bond unit and no tetrahedral carbon with four different substituents. It is achiral, so any mirror images would be superimposable.

Rule out cis-trans isomerism**
For cis-trans you need two different groups on each carbon of the $\text{C=C}$. Here the left carbon carries two identical $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups and the right carbon carries two identical $\text{H}$ atoms. Swapping them gives the same structure, so no stereoisomers exist.

Final answer: Methylpropene is achiral / has no chiral centre, mirror images are superimposable.
One end of the $\text{C=C}$ has two identical $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups and the other end has two identical $\text{H}$ atoms, so no cis-trans isomerism.

hints: Decide whether water or another small molecule is lost when an alkene polymerises, or whether the double bond simply opens.
Draw the monomer $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ then change $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{C-C}$ and add extension bonds on each side.
Check that each carbon in the repeat unit makes four bonds, with two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups on one carbon and two $\text{H}$ atoms on the other.
walkthrough:
Name the polymerisation type**
An alkene forming a poly(alkene) with no small molecule lost is always addition polymerisation. The pi bond breaks and new sigma bonds link monomers.

Build the repeat unit**
Take $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ and open the double bond to a single bond: $-\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}-\text{CH}_{2}-$. Draw the two backbone carbons with bonds extending left and right to show continuation of the chain.

Show all groups clearly**
On the first carbon show two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups, on the second carbon show two $\text{H}$ atoms. Each carbon must be tetravalent. Draw only one repeat unit inside brackets with an n, or with extension bonds.

Final answer: Type: addition (polymerisation).
Repeat unit: $-\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}-\text{CH}_{2}-$ with continuation bonds through the backbone carbons, showing two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups on one carbon and two $\text{H}$ on the other.

hints: Think about the $\text{C-C}$ backbone of poly(alkenes) and whether microbes or water can easily break it down, and what happens if it is burned.
walkthrough:
Link structure to disposal**
Poly(alkenes) have long saturated $\text{C-C}$ chains that are inert to attack by water, acids or microbes. So they persist in landfill for many years and are non-biodegradable. Burning them can release toxic gases like $\text{CO}$ and soot, causing air pollution.
Final answer: Poly(alkenes) are non-biodegradable / give harmful / toxic products on combustion.

hints: For $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$, find the longest chain and the carbon carrying $\text{Br}$, remember the parent is propane with a methyl branch.
For $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Br}$, number the chain to give $\text{Br}$ the lowest number and locate the methyl branch.
walkthrough:
Name the tertiary isomer**
$(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$ has a three carbon propane backbone with a methyl group and a bromine both on carbon 2. So the name is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. This is the Markovnikov product where $\text{Br}$ ends up on the more substituted carbon.

Name the primary isomer**
$(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Br}$ also has a propane backbone with a methyl on carbon 2, but $\text{Br}$ is on carbon 1. Number to give $\text{Br}$ the lowest locant, giving 1-bromo-2-methylpropane. This is the anti-Markovnikov product.

Final answer: $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}$: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
$(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Br}$: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane.
